title: Testing and Estimation of Contextual Generalized Thurstone Models
claim: Normalized test statistics from both model classes stay near a stable threshold across problem sizes, empirically supporting the theoretical scaling.
layout: 1 panel, scatter strips per x value with threshold lines and shaded bands
description: A single scatter plot with n on the x-axis, ranging from 5 to 23 in odd steps, and Normalized Values on the y-axis, from about -0.5 to 2.2. At each n there are two vertical strips of hollow circles: blue for BTL and red for Thurstone. These show the scaled test statistics across many trials, and they spread widely. Two lines with square markers, blue and red, give the estimated thresholds. Each has a translucent shaded band around it. Both lines sit roughly between 0.7 and 0.9 and rise slightly at larger n. A boxed legend in the upper left names the four series. Grid lines cover the whole plot. The eye goes first to the colored lines and bands crossing the dense point clouds.
caption: Scaled test statistics and the estimated thresholds evaluated on the LMSYS dataset.
abstract: Many modern machine learning and artificial intelligence methods utilize preference learning models like Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) to learn latent scores of items based on pairwise comparison data. Despite the successes of such models in specific applications, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), the theoretical justification for the employed models has often been unclear. In this work, we provide a hypothesis testing procedure to test whether a given dataset of pairwise comparisons follows a contextual generalized Thurstone (CGT) model under certain classes of latent functions. The latent functions determine the latent scores, and can be expressed as weighted sums of basis functions. Our CGT model encompasses a wide class of preference learning models, including the popular BTL model. In particular, we prove bounds on critical thresholds for our tests in the minimax sense, which scale like $1/\smash{\sqrt{|\mathcal{E}|^{1/2}k}}$ (where $|\mathcal{E}|$ is the number of edges in the comparison graph and $k$ is the number of observed comparisons per pair) under certain important regimes, such as complete graphs and perfect matchings. Furthermore, to establish our testing results, we also derive error bounds for CGT parameter estimation that generalize and improve on known results in the BTL and non-contextual settings. Finally, we conduct experiments on various synthetic and real-world datasets to verify our theoretical results.
